content: The earlobe, also known as the lobulus auriculæ, is the soft, fleshy lower part of the external ear. It is the lowest portion of the human pinna and extends below the antitragus. Unlike the rest of the pinna, the earlobe lacks cartilage, which makes it less firm and elastic. Instead, it is composed of tough areolar and adipose (fatty) connective tissues. The earlobe has a rich blood supply, which may contribute to warming the ears, but it is generally considered to have no significant biological function. The average length of a human earlobe is approximately 2 cm, and it tends to elongate slightly with age. Earlobes can be classified as either free (hanging freely from the head) or attached (connected directly to the head). This distinction is determined by a simple genetic dominance relationship. Freely hanging earlobes are the dominant trait, while attached earlobes are recessive. Individuals with one dominant allele for free earlobes and one recessive allele for attached earlobes will exhibit the free earlobe phenotype. Statistically, free earlobes are about twice as common in the human population as attached earlobes. Earlobes are typically smooth, but in some cases, they may exhibit creases. Creased earlobes have been associated with certain genetic disorders, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Additionally, earlobe creases have been linked to an increased risk of heart attack and coronary heart disease. However, it is important to note that earlobe creases become more common with age, and older individuals are naturally at a higher risk for heart disease. This age-related factor may partially explain the observed association between earlobe creases and cardiovascular conditions. The earlobe is also rich in nerve endings, making it a sensitive and erogenous zone. Earlobe piercing is the most common form of body piercing worldwide and has been practiced throughout human history. Tearing of the earlobe can occur due to the weight of heavy earrings or accidental trauma, but such tears are generally straightforward to repair. In some cultures, earlobe stretching is practiced, where ornaments are used to gradually enlarge the earlobes. Compared to other parts of the ear, earlobe piercings carry a lower risk of infection. The initial healing period for an earlobe piercing typically lasts 6 to 8 weeks. After this time, earrings can be changed, but if the piercing is left unfilled for an extended period, there is a risk of the hole closing. Even after complete healing, prolonged absence of earrings may cause the piercing to shrink to a smaller size, though it may never fully close.
